clue.text: Picture of photographer saying "cheese"?

parts.note: a self-portrait snapped on a phone shows the person taking it, grinning at their own lens

explanation.surface: A caption request: a shot of a cameraman telling his subjects to smile.
explanation.walkthrough: We expect the photographer to say 'cheese' to others; here the photographer is the subject too.
explanation.definitionFit: A self-taken phone snapshot shows the very person holding the camera, smiling at it.

clue.text: Ambush teacher with award in the auditorium

indicators.note: an auditorium is where an audience hears things, so the words are taken as spoken

parts.note: a teacher is addressed as SIR, and an award is a PRIZE

explanation.surface: A schoolmaster is waylaid on stage at a prize-giving in the school hall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in the auditorium' signals that SIR PRIZE, said out loud, gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To ambush someone is to attack them unexpectedly, catching them off guard.

clue.text: Former city from inland region only half built

indicators.note: built means put together, so these letters are assembled in a new order
only half of the word region is used, its first three letters

explanation.surface: A city that grew up in the interior only half-constructed, now gone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'only half' keeps REG from 'region'; 'built' rearranges INLAND plus REG.
explanation.definitionFit: The Soviet name for St Petersburg, used from 1924 to 1991, so a city name no longer current.

clue.text: Perennial digital assistant returns

indicators.note: returns means the name of the assistant is read backwards

parts.note: Siri is Apple's voice-controlled digital assistant

explanation.surface: An ever-present phone helper keeps coming back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perennial' looks like an adjective about the assistant, but it is a noun: a plant that lives for years.
explanation.definitionFit: This flowering plant regrows every year, making it a garden perennial.

clue.text: Miserable, lousy, cheap tit!

indicators.note: lousy means poor or bad, so the letters of the words that follow are rearranged

explanation.surface: A rant at a stingy, wretched person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lousy' scrambles CHEAPTIT; 'tit' here is the bird or an insult, not a definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe something so feeble or wretched it invites scorn or pity.

clue.text: Not married — ambition I abandoned from the start

indicators.note: abandoned means wild and unrestrained, so the remaining letters are rearranged
Not here means the married letter is left out of the words that follow

explanation.surface: A single person gave up on their ambitions from the outset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not married' removes M from AMBITION I, leaving ABITIONI; 'abandoned' rearranges those letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase is used in English for beginning at the very beginning, from first principles.

clue.text: Help needed after audition for trumpet?

indicators.note: needed after places the help word after the audition word

parts.note: an audition is a hearing, a trial performance before judges
help means aid

explanation.surface: A trumpeter needs assistance once their audition is over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trumpet' is not the instrument but an ear trumpet, the old cone held to the ear; the question mark flags this.
explanation.definitionFit: An ear trumpet was an early device to amplify sound for people who could not hear well.

clue.text: Husband enters drunk, scratching bottom and something else in his trousers

indicators.note: enters means the husband letter goes inside the trimmed word
scratching means deleting, and the bottom of a down entry is its last letter

parts.note: tight is slang for drunk

explanation.surface: A drunken husband comes home scratching his backside, with something else going on in his trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scratching bottom' trims TIGHT to TIGH; 'enters' puts H inside it. The bottom being scratched sounds anatomical but means a last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The upper leg is one more body part found inside a pair of trousers, besides the bottom.

clue.text: This land could be Mohican, a Dakotan discovered

indicators.note: discovered means found lying inside, so the answer is spelled out across the words Mohican, a Dakotan

explanation.surface: A country that a Native American, perhaps from Dakota, might be said to have found.
explanation.walkthrough: 'discovered' signals the letters are found in 'MohiCAN A DAkotan', running across the word breaks.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a North American country, a land neighbouring the Dakotas to the north.

clue.text: Depart in some pain

indicators.note: in means the leaving word is placed inside the word for some

parts.note: any means some, as in 'have you any?'
to depart is to go

explanation.surface: Leaving while suffering a little.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Depart' and 'some' are both plain synonyms; 'in' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Severe suffering, physical or mental, is anguish or torment.

clue.text: Republican Party leader leaves, short of breath and in a rage

indicators.note: leaves means the party letter departs and the Republican letter takes its place

parts.note: someone short of breath is panting

indicators.note: leader means the first letter of the word Party

explanation.surface: A US politician quits his party leadership, gasping and furious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Party leader' is P; 'leaves' swaps it out of PANTING for R (Republican).
explanation.definitionFit: Someone shouting angrily and at length is in a furious temper, raving.

clue.text: I could be a Latin

indicators.note: could be means the letters given might become something else when rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone muses that they may be of Latin stock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'could be' rearranges A LATIN after I; and I is also the international vehicle code for Italy, so the whole clue describes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A person from Italy is one of the Latin peoples, descended from the language of Rome.

clue.text: Complete grade

definitions.meaning: as in 'a ... outsider', meaning utter or absolute
a level or position in a hierarchy, as in military standing

explanation.surface: Two words side by side: finish, and assess.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means utter as an adjective and a level of seniority as a noun.

clue.text: Lacking polish, like this second def

definitions.meaning: not given its final refinement, rough
the word def is a short form of definition, a word left incomplete

explanation.surface: A note on a rough draft whose second definition was never finished.
explanation.walkthrough: The second part is self-referential: 'def' is the start of 'definition', a word cut off before its end.
explanation.definitionFit: Work lacking polish is not completed; 'def' is an incomplete form of a word.

clue.text: Characteristic mood?

definitions.meaning: serving as a sign of something, as in 'typical of'
in grammar, the verb mood that states facts, as opposed to subjunctive or imperative

explanation.surface: Asking whether a typical temperament is in question.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mood' is not a feeling but the grammatical term for a verb form; the question mark flags this.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means suggestive or typical of, and it names the grammatical mood for plain statements.

clue.text: Emerge in season

definitions.meaning: the time of year between winter and summer

explanation.surface: Come out at a certain time of year.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to arise suddenly; the noun is the season when plants begin growing.

clue.text: Hang up band elsewhere

parts.note: a ring is a circular band
off means away or elsewhere, as in 'he's off'

explanation.surface: Hanging a group's poster somewhere else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hang up' sounds like hanging a picture, but it is ending a phone call.
explanation.definitionFit: To end a telephone call is to put down the receiver, a British phrasal verb.

clue.text: Wonderful, but all in the mind

explanation.surface: Something marvellous that turns out to be only imagined.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means superb in everyday speech and imaginary or fanciful in its original sense.

clue.text: Rustic is also part crazy

indicators.note: crazy means wild or disordered, so the letters of the words that follow are rearranged

explanation.surface: A country bumpkin is said to be a little mad as well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crazy' rearranges ALSOPART; 'is' links definition and wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Describing the countryside and simple rural life, especially of shepherds.

clue.text: Lose head in this teary unravelling

definitions.text: Lose head in this teary unravelling

indicators.note: unravelling means coming apart, so the letters are rearranged
Lose head means the first letter of the word this is dropped

explanation.surface: Someone loses their composure in a tearful breakdown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lose head' drops T from THIS, leaving HIS; 'unravelling' rearranges HIS plus TEARY. Read whole, the clue describes the state too.
explanation.definitionFit: Uncontrolled emotional excess, where people panic and weep, is losing one's composure.

clue.text: Almost respect a trainee officer

indicators.note: Almost means the last letter of the respect word is dropped

parts.note: to respect someone is to admire them
L stands for learner, as on British learner-driver plates

explanation.surface: Nearly looking up to a cadet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost' trims ADMIRE to ADMIR; add A and L for learner, the trainee.
explanation.definitionFit: A senior naval commander holds one of the top ranks among officers at sea.

clue.text: Fool with money coming back to get organ

parts.note: to kid someone is to fool them

indicators.note: coming back means the currency word is read backwards

parts.note: the yen is the Japanese currency

explanation.surface: Someone tricks a person into returning cash for a transplant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming back' reverses the Japanese currency; 'money' could be any currency, so the crossers help pick which.
explanation.definitionFit: A body part that filters blood and makes urine is an internal organ.

clue.text: Bold and without limits, they grow rich

indicators.note: without limits means each of the three words loses its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Plucky, and with no ceiling, they become wealthy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without limits' strips the ends from THEY, GROW and RICH, leaving HE, RO, IC.
explanation.definitionFit: Showing great courage and daring is the mark of a brave figure from legend.

clue.text: Westerners in Kalahari organise pleasant jaunt, exploring hill in South Africa

indicators.note: on a map west is on the left, so the westerners are the leftmost, first letters of each word

explanation.surface: Visitors from the West arrange a nice outing in the Kalahari desert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Westerners' looks like tourists but means the leftmost letters of five words.
explanation.definitionFit: A small isolated hill on the South African veld, an Afrikaans word.

clue.text: Stock obtained from one-time purchase

parts.note: ex means former, as in ex-wife
purchase means grip, as does traction

explanation.surface: Shares bought in a single transaction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stock' and 'purchase' suggest shopping; stock is lineage and purchase is grip.
explanation.definitionFit: Stock here means ancestry or descent, a family's origin.

clue.text: Great man is tense when speaking

indicators.note: when speaking means the word is said out loud and the sound gives the letters

parts.note: to tense a muscle is to tighten it

explanation.surface: A towering figure grows nervous whenever he has to make a speech.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tense' looks like an adjective (nervous) but is a verb, tighten; said out loud it gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A giant of Greek myth, and so by extension a person of enormous stature or influence.

clue.text: Idiotic dunderhead back on board

parts.note: the head of the word dunder is its first letter, D
aft means the rear part of a ship

explanation.surface: A fool has returned to the ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dunderhead' looks like a fool but splits into 'dunder' plus 'head', its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe someone silly or foolish, a British colloquial synonym.

clue.text: Doing nothing after output's oddly cut

indicators.note: after places the nothing letter after the remaining letters
oddly cut means the odd-numbered letters of the word output's are removed, keeping the even ones

parts.note: O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Someone idle once their production was halved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddly cut' removes the 1st, 3rd, 5th and 7th letters of OUTPUTS, leaving UPT, with O after it.
explanation.definitionFit: As in 'what are you up to?', meaning what someone is busy with.

clue.text: Dismissed sound of instrument as anomaly

parts.note: a batsman dismissed in cricket is out

indicators.note: sound of means the instrument's name is taken as heard, not as spelt

parts.note: a lyre is a small ancient harp

explanation.surface: Someone rejected a musical sound as an odd one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dismissed' is the cricket sense: a batsman given out. 'sound of' applies only to the instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: A data point far from the rest, or a thing set apart from its group, is an exception.

clue.text: The highest object of Roman worship: a large, almost spherical body

definitions.text: The highest object of Roman worship
definitions.meaning: the king of the Roman gods, counterpart of the Greek Zeus
the biggest planet in the solar system, slightly flattened at the poles

explanation.surface: A description of both a supreme god and a vast celestial globe.
explanation.definitionFit: The name belongs both to the chief Roman deity and to the gas giant named after him.

clue.text: Female carrying drug hidden by inmates — clots!

indicators.note: hidden by means the result is placed inside the inmates word

parts.note: cons is short for convicts, prison inmates

indicators.note: carrying means the female word holds the drug letter inside it

parts.note: gal is a girl, a female
E is short for ecstasy

explanation.surface: A woman smuggles drugs concealed by prisoners, and the narrator calls them all idiots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'carrying' puts E inside the female word, giving GEAL; 'hidden by' puts that inside the inmates. 'clots' looks like the British insult, idiots, but is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: When blood or fat clots, it thickens and sets from liquid into a solid mass.

clue.text: Followed short fellow, I understand

parts.note: to have followed an argument is to have got it

indicators.note: short means the fellow word loses its last letter

parts.note: a chap is a fellow

explanation.surface: Someone trailed a small man and says they see what is going on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Followed' is not trailing but understanding, as in 'I followed what you said'.
explanation.definitionFit: A casual exclamation of comprehension, as in 'got you', meaning the point is grasped.
